newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Brash says evidence of NZ house prices stabilising.
newsitem.headline: Brash says evidence of NZ house prices stabilising.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said on Friday there was evidence house prices in New Zealand were stabilising.

Presenting the bank's six monthly economic projections, Brash said house prices took much of the blame for the forecast of annual underlying inflation rising to 2.7 percent, against the bank's target band of 0-2 percent.

"There is a lot of evidence to suggest that house prices have stabilised in the last little while with some indication that house prices have fallen recently -- not very dramatic falls but then we are not expecting a dramatic fall."
Anecdotal evidence suggested the Auckland market had stabilised, he said, adding that rising house prices were not just an Auckland phenomenon.
Brash said the bank's forecasts assumed a 4-5 percent fall in house prices by the end of 1997.

If the bank's assumption was incorrect, and Brash acknowledged resistance to the notion in some quarters, then inflation would be higher than forecast which in turn would mean monetary policy would have to be firmer than currently projected.
Brash said in the low inflation environment of the 1990s, a fall in real house prices was much more likely to be reflected in a fall in nominal houses prices.

He said because of very strong growth in bank lending to the household sector for housing over the last few years, the RB would be particularly keen to resist any movements in mortgage rates which might reignite house prices.
